posts.topic: waiting 30 minutes after eating before you could swim
posts.on_image: YOU JUST ATE. 30 MINUTES, OR YOU'LL GET A CRAMP AND DROWN.
posts.caption: Every summer Sunday we packed bologna sandwiches and drove down to Table Rock Lake, and every summer Sunday the same thing happened. You'd swallow the last bite, and Mom would look at her watch like she was timing an egg. Thirty minutes. Not twenty-five, not close enough. My brother Kenny and I sat on the end of that dock wrapped in towels, sweating in the July sun, watching other people's kids cannonball in like nobody had warned them. Nobody ever explained what the cramp was or why it only came after lunch. We just knew it was down there in the water, waiting for anybody who'd had a pickle. Kenny once asked if one bite of a Twinkie counted, and Mom started the clock over.
posts.first:
My mother timed it with the same Timex she used for the pot roast, and she never once gave us a minute off for good behavior. I caught myself doing the exact same thing to my own kids at the city pool in 1984. My son still brings it up.

posts.topic: the turkey soup that outlasted the turkey
posts.on_image: THE TURKEY WAS GONE BY SATURDAY. THE TURKEY SOUP LASTED TILL CHRISTMAS.
posts.caption: By the Saturday after Thanksgiving the bird was down to its frame, and that's when Mom got out the big speckled pot. Everything went in. The carcass, two onions, whatever celery was going limp in the crisper, and a handful of egg noodles that never seemed to make it go down. She ladled it out for lunch, then supper, then lunch again. Dad started calling it the eternal flame. Around the second week of December you'd open the Frigidaire and there it was, in a Pyrex dish with a saucer on top. My little brother quietly started eating lunch at his buddy's house.
posts.first:
My grandmother Opal held back the turkey neck from dinner every year just for the soup pot. She said the bones were the best part of the bird, and she meant it. I didn't believe her until I was about forty.

posts.topic: Go ask your father / Go ask your mother
posts.on_image: MOM: GO ASK YOUR FATHER. / DAD: GO ASK YOUR MOTHER.
posts.caption: All I wanted was to sleep over at Jimmy Kowalski's on a Friday night. Mom was at the stove stirring the chili, and she pointed me toward the living room without missing a stir. Go ask your father. So I went in there, and Dad looked at me over the top of the Dayton Daily News and pointed me right back to the kitchen. I made that trip four times. Somewhere around the third lap I figured out they weren't confused. They were waiting for me to give up. I never did get to Jimmy's, but I put about a mile on that kitchen linoleum.
posts.first:
My sister Bonnie cracked the system years before I did. She'd ask Dad first, and when he said go ask your mother, she'd walk in and tell Mom that Dad said it was fine. It worked right up until they compared notes over the dishes.

posts.topic: sneaking in after curfew and Dad clicks on the lamp
posts.on_image: CURFEW WAS MIDNIGHT. HAVE A SEAT.
posts.caption: Curfew was midnight, and I rolled into the driveway at 12:40 with the headlights off, like that ever fooled anybody. I'd dropped Sharon off over on 23rd Avenue and lost track of the time, which is what you tell yourself. I took my loafers off on the porch and eased the front door open about an inch at a time. The house was pitch dark. I got two steps in before I heard that little click, and there was Dad in his chair in his bathrobe, wide awake and calm as a judge. He didn't yell, he just said have a seat, and that was a whole lot worse. I spent forty minutes explaining a flat tire I never had and didn't see the car keys again until the Fourth of July.
posts.first:
Years later Mom told me Dad never went to bed until every one of us was home. He'd sit in that chair with the lights off and listen for a car to turn in. Then he'd reach for the lamp, every single time.

posts.topic: Mom's home perm the night before picture day
posts.on_image: MOM GAVE ME A HOME PERM THE NIGHT BEFORE PICTURE DAY / THAT PICTURE IS STILL ON GRANDMA'S WALL
posts.caption: Mom bought a Toni home permanent at the Rexall and decided the night before school pictures was the perfect time to try it out. The whole house smelled like rotten eggs and ammonia. She rolled my hair up on those little pink rods so tight my eyes watered, while my sister Brenda timed it with the oven timer. When the rods came out, I looked like a dandelion that had been hit by lightning. Mom said it would relax by morning. It did not relax by morning. Grandma ordered the big 8 by 10, framed it, and hung it in her front hallway, where it stayed for thirty years.
posts.first:
Mom gave my cousin Sheila the same perm a year later, so at least I wasn't alone in the family album. Sheila has tried to sneak her picture off Aunt Marlene's piano three different times. Aunt Marlene always finds it and puts it right back.
